One of the built-in Modifier kinds
e: Compose builds a SemanticsTree alongside the UI; tests find nodes via `onNodeWithText` and `onNodeWithTag`. Custom semantics use `Modifier.semantics{}`.

q: What kind of test does this code define?
a: Instrumentation test on a device
Local JVM test for Compose
Standard Espresso UI test on device
Screenshot test through Paparazzi
e: createComposeRule() targets local tests under src/test/. For on-device runs use createAndroidComposeRule (instrumentation tests).

q: How does Paparazzi differ from Roborazzi?
a: Same library shipped under two different names and APIs
Paparazzi has no Android, Roborazzi uses Robolectric
Roborazzi is intended exclusively for iOS UI testing
Paparazzi is just plain unit tests of public API
e: Paparazzi renders Compose/View on the JVM without the Android Framework. Roborazzi uses Robolectric, supports more APIs, and is slower.

q: What does LeakCanary detect in a debug build?
a: ANR events on the main UI thread of the app
Memory leaks via retained objects
Network errors from the OkHttp/HTTP client
Crash reports inside the release build
e: LeakCanary watches Activity, Fragment and View after destroy and uses WeakReference plus GC to find retained leaks, printing the chain to GC root.

q: What does StrictMode do on Android?
a: Forbids any release build at all
Catches I/O and leaks in debug
Encrypts SharedPreferences data
Forces the R8 minifier to run
e: StrictMode is a debug tool: ThreadPolicy catches I/O on the main thread; VmPolicy catches leaked closeables, untagged sockets, etc. Disabled in release.

q: What is the best way to debug HTTP traffic inside the app?
a: LeakCanary inside a debug build
Chucker, an OkHttp interceptor
ProGuard rules for the reflection
MockK swapping out the services
e: Chucker is an OkHttp interceptor that displays requests inside the app itself. Alternatives: Charles, Stetho, Flipper — but Chucker needs no proxy.

q: How does R8 fundamentally differ from ProGuard in an Android build?
a: Only renames classes and fields without doing any shrinking
Combines shrinking, obfuscation and dexing in one pass
Operates only on resources and asset folders during build
Replaces the D8 dexer step while still using ProGuard
e: R8 is the successor to ProGuard: in a single pass it does tree-shaking, obfuscation and emits DEX directly, skipping the intermediate .class to .dex step.

q: What does resource shrinking in R8/AGP cover, and which flag enables it?
a: Setting minifyEnabled true on its own is already enough
shrinkResources true together with minifyEnabled true
Toggling useProguard true and adding the right keep rules
Listing resConfigs en in the defaultConfig block of Gradle
e: shrinkResources only works when minifyEnabled is on. R8 builds the graph of used resources and Gradle drops unreachable drawables, strings and layouts.

q: What happens if R8 keep rules omit @Keep for a class accessed only via reflection?
a: The build fails immediately at the link step with a missing-symbol error
Class is renamed or stripped, reflection throws ClassNotFoundException
R8 detects the reflective access automatically and keeps the class intact
Only a build warning is emitted and runtime behaviour is unaffected
e: R8 cannot see Class.forName/getDeclaredMethod usage, so without @Keep or a -keep rule the class is obfuscated or removed entirely.

q: What is the key advantage of Android Keystore over storing a key in a plain file?
a: Keys are encrypted with a password derived from the app signing certificate
Private key never leaves secure storage (TEE/StrongBox), app gets a handle
Keys are backed up and synced across devices through the user's Google account
Keystore runs raw AES operations faster than equivalent userspace crypto code
e: Crypto operations run inside TEE/StrongBox and the app holds an opaque handle, so raw key material cannot be extracted from process memory.

q: What does this code do on the first and on subsequent launches?
a: Generates a brand new key on every launch and overwrites the old one
Creates the key once, then reuses the existing one by alias
Crashes on the second launch because the alias is already taken
Returns null until the previous alias is removed manually first
e: KeyStore.getInstance("AndroidKeyStore") persists keys across runs. If the alias already exists, KeyGenerator will not recreate it without an explicit delete.

q: Which encryption schemes does EncryptedSharedPreferences use by default?
a: AES128_SIV for keys and AES256_GCM for values
AES256_SIV for keys and AES256_GCM for values
RSA wrapping for keys and AES256_CBC for values
ChaCha20-Poly1305 applied to keys and to values
e: Backed by Tink: AES256_SIV (deterministic, so lookups by key work) for pref names, and AES256_GCM (randomized) for values.

q: What is wrong with this way of obtaining encrypted SharedPreferences?
a: Nothing is wrong, this is the recommended snippet today
MasterKeys.AES256_GCM_SPEC is deprecated, use MasterKey.Builder
It must pass context.applicationContext explicitly to avoid leaks
Pref file names are not allowed to contain underscore characters
e: MasterKeys and AES256_GCM_SPEC are deprecated since security-crypto 1.1.0. Use MasterKey.Builder(context).setKeyScheme(AES256_GCM).build().
code:
val keyAlias = MasterKeys.getOrCreate(MasterKeys.AES256_GCM_SPEC)
val prefs = EncryptedSharedPreferences.create(
    "secure_prefs", keyAlias, context,
    PrefKeyEncryptionScheme.AES256_SIV,
    PrefValueEncryptionScheme.AES256_GCM
)

q: Why is BiometricPrompt preferred over the legacy FingerprintManager?
a: It only restyles the dialog's accent color and title typography
Unified across biometrics, supports CryptoObject and credential fallback
It runs noticeably faster than the older fingerprint API on every device
It needs no runtime permission and no manifest declaration of any kind
e: BiometricPrompt abstracts face/fingerprint/iris, integrates with Keystore via CryptoObject and provides a system UI with PIN/pattern fallback.

q: What does network_security_config with cleartextTrafficPermitted="false" plus pin-set enforce?
a: Blocks plain HTTP and pins to a specific certificate SPKI hash
Disables TLS validation entirely so any server cert is accepted
Routes all application traffic through the system-managed VPN tunnel
Trusts any self-signed certificate presented by the remote endpoint
e: Network Security Config declaratively blocks cleartext and enforces public-key pinning: the connection aborts if the server cert hash matches no pin.

q: Which API does Google currently recommend for device and app integrity attestation?
a: SafetyNet Attestation API used with the legacy nonce flow
Play Integrity API with server-side token verification
RootBeer-style local heuristic library checks bundled in
DeviceAdmin policy API combined with custom integrity checks
e: SafetyNet Attestation has been deprecated since 2023. The server should validate Play Integrity tokens, which cover device, app and licensing checks.

q: Which ML Kit detector runs fully on-device and needs no internet connection?
a: Cloud Text Recognition routed through the Vision endpoint
Barcode Scanning, Face Detection, On-device Text Recognition
Smart Reply requested through the Cloud API gateway only
All ML Kit detectors require an active network link to function
e: ML Kit splits into on-device APIs (barcode, face, pose, latin text recognition, smart reply) and cloud-based ones. On-device APIs work offline and are free.

q: Why quantize a TFLite model down to int8?
a: It improves the model's overall accuracy on the held-out validation set
Shrinks size around 4x and speeds up CPU/NPU inference via integer math
Makes the model portable across runtimes without any conversion at all
It is mandatory for any GPU delegate to compile and execute the graph
e: Post-training int8 quantization compresses weights float32 to int8 (around 4x) and uses SIMD/INT accelerators. The cost is a small accuracy drop, usually under 1%.

q: What happens if you call interpreter.run() on the main thread for a heavy model?
a: Nothing bad happens, the TFLite runtime is fully asynchronous internally
Synchronous blocking inference on the UI thread triggers an ANR
It fails to compile against the published TFLite SDK on Android entirely
TFLite silently moves the call onto an internal background worker thread
e: Interpreter.run() is a synchronous CPU/GPU call. For non-trivial models use Dispatchers.Default or a TaskRunner, otherwise you get jank or an ANR.
code:
val interpreter = Interpreter(loadModelFile("model.tflite"),
    Interpreter.Options().apply { setNumThreads(4) })
val input = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(1*224*224*3*4).order(ByteOrder.nativeOrder())
val output = Array(1) { FloatArray(1000) }
interpreter.run(input, output)

q: Which TFLite delegate gives the best gains on modern Android devices with an NPU?
a: GPU delegate built on top of OpenGL or OpenCL backends
NNAPI delegate (Android 8.1+) or a native NPU SDK
XNNPACK CPU delegate with multi-threaded fused ops
Hexagon delegate (Snapdragon-only, now deprecated)
e: NNAPI dispatches ops to available accelerators (NPU/DSP/GPU) through the OS. On Pixel/Tensor and many SoCs it beats the pure GPU delegate.

q: What is an Anchor in ARCore?
a: A texture atlas bound to a rendered model placed inside the scene
A fixed pose in the world, kept consistent as tracking refines
The currently active hardware camera component on the host device
A periodic light-estimation result attached to the current AR frame
e: An Anchor is a stable attachment to a real-world point. ARCore corrects its coordinates as SLAM drifts so the virtual object does not slide away.

q: Which ARSession lifecycle step is required before every render frame?
a: Calling session.pause() before drawing to flush internal state
session.update() returns a Frame with fresh tracking data
Calling session.close() to release the camera between frames
Reconfiguring HDR settings on the session for each new frame
e: Each frame GLSurfaceView.onDrawFrame calls session.update(); the returned Frame exposes camera, planes and anchors. Without update the data goes stale.

q: Pose detection in ML Kit returns a PoseLandmark with which fields?
a: Just the x and y screen coordinates of the landmark point
position3D (x,y,z), inFrameLikelihood and a landmark type
A 2D bounding box around the detected person in the frame
Only an overall confidence score for the whole pose result
e: Each of the 33 landmarks carries a 3D position (z relative to the hips, in pixels), an in-frame likelihood and a type (NOSE, LEFT_SHOULDER, etc.).

q: When is on-device inference preferable to a cloud endpoint?
a: Always, regardless of the model size, latency target or device constraints
When latency, privacy or offline matter; APK size and CPU pay the cost
Only for very small toy models embedded in tutorial code and demo apps
Only available to apps subscribed to a paid Google Cloud service tier plan
e: On-device wins on privacy and latency but bundles the model and burns battery/CPU. Cloud is preferred for heavy models and centralized updates.

q: How do you correctly wire an ML Kit detector to CameraX in Compose or Views?
a: Through the ImageCapture use case and its takePicture result callback
Via ImageAnalysis.Analyzer and InputImage.fromMediaImage with rotation
Only through the VideoCapture use case bound to the current lifecycle owner
ML Kit detectors are not compatible with the CameraX library on Android
e: ImageAnalysis emits ImageProxy then InputImage.fromMediaImage(image, rotationDegrees). After detector.process() you must call imageProxy.close() or backpressure builds up.

q: What sets Yandex MapKit apart from the Google Maps SDK on Android?
a: Yandex MapKit is built on top of OpenStreetMap raw tile data
Own engine and API, stronger RU coverage: traffic, transit, panoramas
Both SDKs are fully API-compatible and use the same MapView types
Yandex MapKit only works while the device has an active network connection
e: MapKit is an independent SDK with MapView/MapObjectCollection. Its API is not Google Maps compatible; it has stronger RU/CIS coverage, traffic and transit data.

q: How does Android Auto fundamentally differ from Android Automotive OS?
a: They are essentially the same Google product under two marketing names
Auto projects from the phone; Automotive OS is the car's own Android
Android Automotive OS is exclusive to Tesla-branded vehicles and prototypes
Android Auto runs entirely on the head unit without any paired phone link
e: Android Auto projects the phone UI onto the IVI head unit. Android Automotive OS is the car's own OS (Polestar, Volvo); apps install directly via Play.

q: What is the Car App Library and what is it used for?
a: A general-purpose Material UI kit aimed at phones and large tablets
Jetpack library for templated nav/POI/IOT screens on Auto and AAOS
An ORM and persistence layer tailored to live vehicle telemetry data
A Compose-based replacement for the legacy car projection UI runtime
e: androidx.car.app exposes a limited set of templates (ListTemplate, NavigationTemplate) certified for driver safety. Arbitrary custom UI is forbidden.

q: Which library powered the classic 10-foot UI on Android TV before Compose?
a: AndroidX Leanback (BrowseFragment, RowsSupportFragment)
Material Components for Android with TV-specific themes
AppCompat with a custom action bar and drawer styling
ConstraintLayout combined with manual D-pad focus handling
e: Leanback is the standard for D-pad TV navigation: BrowseSupportFragment, HeadersFragment, Presenter/PresenterSelector. Compose for TV now sits alongside it.

q: What is a Tile in Wear OS 3+?
a: A small interactive widget shown on the paired Android phone
A swipeable summary page next to the watch face, via ProtoLayout
A push-style notification variant designed for wearable devices
A long-running background service that polls user health metrics
e: A Tile is a lightweight pre-rendered screen alongside the watch face. It is implemented through a TileService and declarative ProtoLayout, not the Compose runtime.

q: Why use the Health Services API on Wear OS instead of the raw Sensor API?
a: They are essentially the same API exposed under two different package names
Battery-aware sensor aggregation with passive/active and unified metrics
Required by Google in order to upload any health data into the cloud backend
Available only to certified medical-grade watches and approved partner hardware
e: Health Services abstracts heterogeneous sensors, exposes ExerciseClient/PassiveMonitoringClient and is battery-optimized. Sensor API gives raw data without aggregation.

q: Which API reports a foldable's posture (table-top, book, flat)?
a: DisplayManager via display metrics and refresh-rate listener observers
Jetpack WindowManager: WindowInfoTracker plus FoldingFeature.State
Configuration.smallestScreenWidthDp checked at runtime on every frame
ActivityManager process info APIs combined with raw sensor heuristics
e: WindowInfoTracker.windowLayoutInfo emits Flow<WindowLayoutInfo> with FoldingFeature: state (HALF_OPENED/FLAT), orientation (HORIZONTAL/VERTICAL) and bounds.

q: Which mechanism is used to exchange data between a Wear OS watch and the paired phone?
a: A direct raw Bluetooth socket opened by the application itself
Wearable Data Layer API (DataClient, MessageClient, NodeClient)
REST round-trips routed through a backend server on the internet
A wired USB tether between the watch and the paired phone device
e: Data Layer syncs DataItems (eventually consistent), sends MessageEvents (fire-and-forget) and discovers nodes via NodeClient. It runs over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi.

q: What is a Complication in Wear OS?
a: A decorative animation effect rendered on the watch face surface
A data slot on the watch face fed by ComplicationDataSourceService
An error state of the watch-and-phone pairing reported to the user
A visual theme bundle with colors and typography for the watch face
e: Complications are typed data sources (SHORT_TEXT, RANGED_VALUE, ICON and so on). The watch face declares slots and the user wires any app's source into them.

q: What is required to implement a watch face on modern Wear OS 3+?
a: A static PNG resource bundled inside the watch face APK package itself
WatchFaceService (androidx.wear.watchface) with Renderer and UserStyle
A standard Activity packaged as the launcher entry of the watch app
A foreground Service combined with periodic AlarmManager wakeups per minute
e: The modern API is androidx.wear.watchface: WatchFaceService then WatchFace(Renderer) supporting interactive/ambient modes, complication slots and user style.

q: Which API drives content output to both built-in and external displays (multi-display)?
a: DisplayManager + ActivityOptions.setLaunchDisplayId / Presentation API
WindowManager on its own without any flags or extra configuration here
MediaRouter alone, intended only for screen casting and audio output routing
Direct calls into SurfaceFlinger from the application process itself at runtime
e: DisplayManager enumerates displays; Presentation draws a separate root view on the second screen, and ActivityOptions.setLaunchDisplayId launches an Activity there.
